messages.subject: Ree and Sanmartin critique
parts:
Hi,
I was wondering if you are able to give any clarification or advice about using (and comparing) the Dec and Dec+J models in light of the critique by Ree and Sanmartin and how to pre-empt potential objections
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jbi.13173

I notice your coauthored 2019 paper with Kristina Klaus takes issue with these arguments but I didn't find the review of these objections in the supplementary material that seemed to be mentioned.
https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/advance-article/doi/10.1093/sysbio/syz034/5490843

As well as the question of statistical comparison between these models, I am interested in the implication that ancestral reconstructions using Dec or Dec+J would be unreliable because these models do not treat cladogenic events as probabilistic and are therefore systematically biased towards interpreting range changes using cladogenetic events rather than anagetic change.

Many thanks

messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Ree and Sanmartin critique
parts:
Hi -- sorry for the slow reply on this. As said on Twitter back when this critique came out: ( https://twitter.com/nickjmatzke/status/965319092050657280 ) I would dearly love to develop a community of biogeographers who are critical thinkers about about models and model comparison. 

In my view, the problems with the Ree/Sanmartin critique are epic, fundamental, and obvious, but over the last year, it has become clear that many people feel ill-equipped to judge the issue themselves, and instead default to "authorities disagree".  This is a general problem in the field, I'm afraid. 

I do have a looooong draft response to the RS critique, but the feedback I've gotten is that it is too long and dense to be effective.  It's challenging to shorten it, since there are so many different issues to cover, and then I had an international move, a new job, and a baby, so it has been tough to get back to it.

Anyway, in order to help the goal of "developing a community of biogeographers who are critical thinkers about models and model comparison", it seems like, rather than having me just blast out a counter-critique, it would make sense to help people think through the issues themselves.  I proposed to Bruce that I ask a Socratic-type question, and then he and others can post answers, and then we can discuss. I encourage others to pitch in.

Let's start with this:

On Tue, Nov 19, 2019 at 1:03 AM Bruce Murphy <brucea...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi,
I was wondering if you are able to give any clarification or advice about using (and comparing) the Dec and Dec+J models in light of the critique by Ree and Sanmartin and how to pre-empt potential objections
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jbi.13173

The first question I think anyone considering the critique should ask themselves is,

Q: Are the likelihood calculations presented in the Ree/Sanmartin critique correct?

RS start with a 2-taxon tree, where one species lives A, and the other lives in B.

They state that the maximized log-likelihoods under DEC and DEC+J are:

DEC:     lnL = -2.890
DEC+J: lnL = -0.693

We can check these by running this tree & geography data in both Lagrange DEC, and BioGeoBEARS-DEC and BioGeoBEARS-DEC+J.

I'm attaching the input files & setups for these runs in Python Lagrange, C++ Lagrange, and BioGeoBEARS.  What likelihoods do these programs report on this dataset?

Cheers,
Nick

PS other short answers:

I notice your coauthored 2019 paper with Kristina Klaus takes issue with these arguments but I didn't find the review of these objections in the supplementary material that seemed to be mentioned.
https://academic.oup.com/sysbio/advance-article/doi/10.1093/sysbio/syz034/5490843

I mentioned this to Bruce already, but for others:

The Supp. Mat. is on Dryad, here: 
https://datadryad.org/stash/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.d117b3k

Inside the zipfile, you want this PDF:
Klaus_Matzke_2019_SysBio_Supplemental_Text.pdf

As well as the question of statistical comparison between these models, I am interested in the implication that ancestral reconstructions using Dec or Dec+J would be unreliable because these models do not treat cladogenic events as probabilistic and are therefore systematically biased towards interpreting range changes using cladogenetic events rather than anagetic change.

Many thanks

Treating cladogenetic events as probabilistic is trivial -- all you have to do is assume the phylogenetic tree was generated by a Yule process (pure-birth), and add this likelihood to the likelihood of the biogeography data.  The resulting inference will be identical, and the Yule likelihood is identical when added to either DEC or DEC+J, so does not make a difference for comparing these models, or for the ancestral range probabilities.

However -- as I have said many times, the real problem here is that lineage extinction is left out. A Yule process means 0 extinction, which means DEC, DEC+J, etc. are assuming that the tree is the complete tree. This is clearly wrong, but then, ignoring or underestimating extinction is an endemic problem in macroevolutionary models based on molecular data.  Whether it has a fatal impact on inference depends on the specific question -- the simulations in Matzke (2014) suggest that it doesn't, at least if extinction is random. See discussions of this issue from years back:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-validation#DEC_DECj

Cheers,
Nick
